items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: were a lot of critics and historians that I take issue with because they are not of the same mold like the Leonard Feathers or the Dan Morgensterns.

ctx.x: Yes. So he lived in the house, and she’s like my sister you know. And Billy Fraser, Slide Hampton, all of us, Freddie Hubbard, we all lived in that house. And there was so much music and Yusef Lateef and all kinds of people would come through the house. And Coltrane and I used to go out to Coltrane’s house and hang out with him. I knew him man, I knew this guy. And he was so beautiful and so focused. Sonny Rollins man, Wynton Kelly man, all these guys man, Philly Jo Jones took me on like a little brother, taught…

were a lot of critics and historians that I take issue with because they are not of the same mold like the Leonard Feathers or the Dan Morgensterns. They don’t have the same kind of humbleness and the same kind of commitment. Some woman came up to me the other day because she was very disturbed about what Oscar Peterson said at the gala the other day. And she asked me, “What do you think about that?” I said, “He was absolutely on the money.” She said, “What?” I said, “Yes, he was telling you the truth. I mean…

Have we kind of created a conflict then with jazz education is now a big business with publications and method books and all that. And this gathering here obviously is positive in some aspects for the music, but is it creating too many of the people you’re talking about that just are spinning out what the book says?

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It included Larry Ridley, whom I had known for a long time before coming to Rutgers

ctx.x: . . . SETA, which was a training program for – she was from Jamaica. She was a charming person who, again, caught on quickly. She had a great telephone manner. She was good at taking messages. She was well organized. Jeanette. She was very good in that position. We got Vincent a scholarship to go to library school at Rutgers. He became a librarian. We eventually – we were a freestanding unit at that point in time. We had an advisory board. It included Larry Ridley, whom I had known for a long time before coming…

an appropriate facility. That was a great step forward. It also gave us more visibility within Rutgers itself and with the outside world. There was a very nice piece done by the then New York Times jazz critic Peter Watrous on the Institute with a photograph of me with a bunch of instruments. We have a big collection of instruments that belonged to famous musicians.
